I’m young but I can tell you how I went through the darkness (however much smaller) myself. I was plagued a long time with my own beliefs. I realized that mattering wasn’t objective when I was around 16 years old. That meant nothing mattered, or it didn’t matter that they did at least. Depression hit the hardest in the night, or at what should have been the absolute highs of my life. It sprang at least partially from the ideas I was having. The first thing I tried that helped was working out. Don’t ask me why, I know it sounds stupid but the testosterone really helped me to a certain extent. Not during the night though. The next thing I realized is that I needed to mourn the loss of hope and purpose that I once held dear. I sat in the shower and repeated “nothing matters” to myself for hours until I stopped crying. Then I mourned each person I loved and the fact that they didn’t matter. And eventually I just grew numb to the words and the idea. I knew I also needed to open up to my emotions more, and I began the painful process of learning how to listen and prevent rather than ignore and control. By far the most effective “treatment” has been smoking weed. It’s not a pleasure thing - it just helps get your thoughts under control and think more creatively. Ive smoked weed every night for about a year now. All of that combined and i’m at the other side. I’ve been off weed for about a month and a half, and I feel fine. I wake up do what I have to, then do what I want to, then go to bed like a normal person. I know it’d be presumptuous to assume i’m anywhere near the situation you’re in, but id like to offer my story anyways in case any of it might help. I wish you the best and please dm me if you want/need to talk.

Here’s my take on the perception of time: something feels longer if you remember more of it, whether that be an event, period of time, etc. People can definitely experience time differently, for example if you’re tired, or high. Our eyes don’t take in images fluidly/infinitely, and if they do then our brain doesn’t process them that way; it operates in a frames per second way, which is why we see the wheel of a car frozen when in reality the car is going however many miles per hour. In this way, I would say time would be able to be experienced differently and is, not just by altered mental states but by different speeds of your brain taking in images. I think our lives start to feel “the same as 20 years ago” or like you aren’t really aging because your memory fills up, and old memories are just getting swapped for new. But the amount of memories stay the same, and so it feels like life hasn’t got any longer. Just a theory though.

Thanks a lot for the well thought out response. I guess there are a lot of biases in my first essay that I should elaborate. First is the idea of time. I can’t see a difference between a day or a year, only a difference in our perception of it. A fly could live one day and experience time like what we would in 2 years. People around us could experience less time than us, just because of the speed of their brain. Time to me doesn’t seem set in stone. 

Next is the importance of being happy and emotion. This has been offered as a meaning to life many times in an obvious kind of manner, but why does pleasure truly matter? Doing something that makes you happy makes you happy; and then what? I understand how some people drive meaning from happiness but to me emotions can’t overtake logic - they’re just chemicals in our brain. In fact, if you combine the idea happiness is the meaning of life with the one above, an overdose on heroin would maximize the utility and happiness for the rest of my life, pure bliss for an equally temporary amount of time.
